issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is poorly matched to the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. 'People in uniform' more strongly suggests assault/police/military trauma than a pediatric medical crisis, and there are no accompanying medical or hospital-related cues to make this clinically coherent.

issues.item: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: 'Revenge ... get even with assailant' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type because a child's life-threatening illness does not ordinarily involve an identifiable assailant. This item is therefore implausible for this trauma context.

issues.item: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'child's life-threatening illness,' revenge against an assailant is clinically incoherent because this trauma does not ordinarily involve a perpetrator to 'get even with.' A clinician would strongly question whether this item belongs to the same trauma narrative.

issues.item: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination implies a perpetrator/interpersonal harm frame ('what other people have done to me') that does not fit the listed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, unless there were unusual circumstances not reflected anywhere else in the profile. This creates a hard-to-explain mismatch with the trauma context and with the trigger items, which are hospital/illness-related.

issues.item: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy item about revenge against an assailant is not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, which does not normally involve a discrete assailant to get even with.

issues.item: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: The other-blame rumination item also implies an interpersonal perpetrator framework ('what other people have done to me') that clashes with the trauma type and with the trigger set, which is dominated by hospital/medical and somatic cues. Together these maladaptive strategy items suggest an assault-like trauma narrative rather than a child's medical crisis.

issues.item: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy item about revenge against an assailant is not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness; this wording implies an interpersonal assault context rather than a medical trauma.

issues.item: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination is possible in medical trauma, but in this profile it is framed as 'what other people have done to me,' which shifts the trauma narrative toward personal victimization rather than distress about a child's illness, making it hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

For trauma type 'child's life-threatening illness,' a burnt-smell danger cue is hard to reconcile clinically unless the illness involved fire/burning, which is not suggested by the trauma context. The hospital/antiseptic trigger fits, but burnt smell appears implausibly tied to a different trauma context.

issues.item: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: 'Revenge against assailant' is strongly incongruent with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, which does not involve an assailant. This item implies an interpersonal assault/attack trauma and is not clinically coherent with the given trauma type.

issues.item: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: 'Revenge against assailant' is not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness; this item implies an interpersonal assault/perpetrator trauma that does not fit the trauma type.

issues.item: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'I dwell on what other people have done to me' similarly frames the trauma as interpersonal victimization by others, which is hard to reconcile with a child's medical crisis unless there were explicit malpractice/perpetrator elements, which are not present elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Boon-Nam Thongchai is a 47-year-old Thai-American man who has worked as a park ranger in a Pacific Northwest state park for the past eleven years. He is married and presents for his initial intake with a PCL-5 score of 72, indicating severe posttraumatic stress symptomatology. The events that precipitated his current difficulties occurred approximately fourteen months ago, when his nine-year-old son, Kiet, was rushed to the emergency room following a sudden and catastrophic diabetic crisis that had gone undetected until the boy collapsed at home. Boon-Nam was the one who found him - unresponsive on the kitchen floor - and rode with him in the ambulance. At the hospital, he stood in a corridor outside a treatment bay while staff worked on Kiet for what he later described as the longest forty minutes of his life. The room carried the sharp, antiseptic smell that he would later come to associate entirely with that corridor, that waiting, that not-knowing. At one point a nurse brushed past him carrying a tray of alcohol swabs, and the smell cut through the air just as a physician emerged to tell him that Kiet's blood glucose had been critically low and that they had nearly lost him. Boon-Nam felt the floor tilt beneath him; he gripped a wall rail as dizziness overtook him. Kiet survived and recovered fully, but something in Boon-Nam did not recover with him.

In the months that followed, Boon-Nam found that his body had retained the logic of that corridor in ways he could not override. When he experiences dizziness now - from standing up too quickly, from dehydration on a long trail patrol, from the physical demands of his outdoor work - the sensation carries an immediacy that belongs entirely to that hospital floor. He does not simply feel dizzy; he is, for a moment, back at the wall rail, certain that something catastrophic is unfolding. The smell of antiseptic cleaning products used in the ranger station bathrooms, or the alcohol-based hand sanitiser mounted by the visitor centre entrance, produces a similar response. He has begun taking longer routes through the station to avoid the sanitiser dispenser, a habit that his colleagues have noticed without understanding.

What has consumed Boon-Nam most persistently, however, is not fear but a grinding, recursive anger. He had come to believe, in the weeks after Kiet's hospitalisation, that the crisis could have been caught earlier - that a routine check-up appointment three months prior had been handled carelessly, that warning signs had been dismissed. He dwells on this with a tenacity that exhausts him. He replays conversations with the paediatrician, rehearses what he should have demanded, constructs and reconstructs scenarios in which he confronts the doctor, the clinic, the system. He is certain that someone failed his son deliberately or through negligence so profound it amounts to the same thing. He spends evenings in a state of internal argument - building cases, imagining reckonings - while his wife, Malee, sits beside him on the couch and cannot reach him. She has tried, on several occasions, to talk through what happened, to name what she went through that night too, and each time Boon-Nam has shut the conversation down. Being reminded of the event by others, even by her, feels intolerable to him in a way he struggles to articulate - as though the account coming from outside him strips away whatever control he still holds over it.

Over the past year, the distance between Boon-Nam and Malee has widened in ways that have become impossible to ignore. She finally told him, two weeks ago, that she was frightened - not of him, but for him. It was this, more than anything else, that brought him to seek help. He arrived at the intake appointment guarded and precise, describing his symptoms with the methodical calm of a man accustomed to writing incident reports. What he is most afraid of, when pressed, is that the anger will never leave him. What he is most hoping for, though he said it quietly, is to be present in his own home again.
